scenes.title: Every ingredient is a share of the flour
scenes.narration: Here is the thing most bread recipes do not tell you. Every ingredient is really just a percentage of the flour.

steps.say: The flour is always one hundred percent. Say we use 500 grams.
Water is sixty six percent of that, so 330 grams.
Salt is two percent, 10 grams.
And yeast is one point two percent, just 6 grams.
Add the percentages up and you get more than a hundred, 169.2.
That is fine. It just means the dough weighs 846 grams.

scenes.title: Hydration is water over flour
scenes.narration: The most important number in that list is the water. Bakers call it hydration.

steps.say: It is just the water divided by the flour. 330 over 500 is sixty six percent.
And that one number tells you how the dough will feel before you even touch it.

scenes.narration: So what changes if you go drier or wetter? Here is the same flour at sixty and at eighty percent.

steps.say: Only 100 grams of water separate these two.
At sixty percent the dough is firm and easy to handle. At eighty it is slack and sticky.
The drier one bakes up tight and chewy. The wetter one is moister inside, and stays fresh longer.
But a wet dough takes more skill to shape, and longer in the oven.
Which is why bagels and pretzels are stiff doughs, and big rustic loaves are wet ones.
Sixty six sits comfortably in between.

scenes.title: Scale the flour, and the rest follows
scenes.narration: And here is why bakers love percentages. Scaling a recipe stops being a headache.

steps.say: Want two loaves? Double the flour, and every other number doubles with it.
Want exactly 1200 grams of dough for a big pan? Divide it by one point six nine two, the total percentage.
That gives 709 grams of flour, and the percentages do the rest.

scenes.title: One lean loaf, step by step
scenes.narration: Now the method. The times come from a tested recipe for this same kind of dough.

steps.say: Mix everything and knead for about 6 minutes, until it is smooth.
Cover it and let it rise until it has doubled. That takes one to two hours, depending on how warm your kitchen is.
Shape it into a loaf.
Let it rise again, about 45 minutes.
Bake it hot, four hundred and fifty Fahrenheit, for twenty to twenty five minutes.
And let it cool before you cut it. It is still cooking inside.

scenes.title: Most of the time, you wait
scenes.narration: Put those times on a clock, taking the quick end of each one.

steps.say: The mixing and kneading is about 6 minutes of work.
Then you wait an hour while the yeast does its thing, and shape it.
In a cool kitchen it can take two, which pushes the bread back to 3 hours 16 minutes.

draw.write: cool kitchen: +1 h, bread at 3 h 16

steps.say: Another forty five minutes of waiting, and into the oven.
About two and a quarter hours from start to bread.
And for 77 percent of that, you are not doing anything at all.
